title: How Prideful Is Your Team?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership note argues that great teams are prideful teams, because pride builds belonging, loyalty, unity, motivation and commitment. It names four sources of pride: the quality of the work, the higher purpose or social value of the work, the history and reputation of the enterprise, and the skills and expertise of colleagues. Leaders who push only performance and goals without tying them to these sources limit the benefit of pride. The best leaders strengthen pride deliberately, praising craftsmanship rather than only the number hit, explaining the purpose behind goals, telling stories of the organization's best moments and pointing out colleagues' expertise. The piece distinguishes team pride from arrogance, saying it raises the standard a team holds for itself. Research is cited suggesting prideful teams correct mistakes faster and attract talented people who want to belong.
points: Team pride comes from four sources: work quality, higher purpose, organizational history and reputation, and colleague expertise.
Leaders who stress results without connecting them to those sources forfeit much of the benefit pride provides.
Pride is built by habit, for example by praising craftsmanship, explaining social purpose, retelling the organization's best moments and naming colleagues' expertise.
Team pride is not arrogance, since it pushes teams to hold themselves to a higher standard and accept critical feedback.
The payoff is retention and quality, because proud teams reportedly correct mistakes faster and attract talented colleagues.
quotes: Pride comes from four primary sources: the quality of the work, the higher purpose or social value of the work, the history and reputation of the enterprise, and the skills and expertise of colleagues.
Leaders who emphasize performance and goal attainment without connecting those outcomes to one or more of the four sources limit the benefits of team pride.
When a project succeeds, they talk about the craftsmanship behind it, not just the number it hit. When the goal is set, they explain the higher purpose it will serve and why that matters socially.
Team pride is not arrogance. Prideful teams don’t look down on others or resist critical feedback. Instead, pride raises the standard a team holds for itself.
Research suggests prideful teams correct mistakes faster, defend their reputation through their behavior, and attract talented colleagues who want to belong to something admired.
Leaders who connect every win to quality, purpose, legacy, or colleague competence give their teams something more lasting than good results. They give them a reason to be proud and a reason to stay.
